source: Zhou et al. (2026, Nature) General scales unlock AI evaluation with explanatory and predictive power
finding: Across 15 LLMs, knowledge-demand abilities are mostly set by model size, while quantitative and logical reasoning, identifying relevant information, and mind modelling rise in chain-of-thought, inference-heavy models (o1, DeepSeek-R1-Distilled). So extra thinking at inference lifts some abilities, not all.
numbers: 15 LLMs on the ADeLe battery (16,108 instances, 20 benchmarks). Reasoning gains show on the two QL scales, MCr and MS; they appear even for the 7B distilled models. Knowledge scales are lower for small and distilled models. o1 overall accuracy 0.843; Babbage-002 0.102.
quote: knowledge dimensions are high for larger models and reduced for small and distilled models
limits: Model-to-model comparison (o1 vs non-reasoning families, R1-distilled vs others), not the same model with and without a scaffold. Training differs as well as inference compute. Profiles are read from text and figure descriptions; no per-dimension effect sizes were extracted.
agent_relevance: Best evidence so far for gap 1: inference-time reasoning acts on a subset of abilities (reasoning, relevance filtering, social inference) and leaves knowledge at the size-set level. A scaffold should be expected to help reasoning-type items and not knowledge-limited ones.

source: Zhou et al. (2026, Nature) ADeLe predictive power
finding: Item-level demand annotations predict per-item success, also on new tasks and new benchmarks, better than embedding or fine-tuned-LLaMA predictors.
numbers: In-distribution accuracy-weighted AUROC about 0.84, ECE 0.01 (GPT-4o best at 0.882; small models less predictable). Task-out-of-distribution weighted AUROC 0.81 (ECE 0.02) vs 0.79 LLaMA and 0.74 GloVe. Benchmark-out-of-distribution 0.75 (ECE 0.04); the other two drop more.
limits: Predicts success of a fixed model on an item. It does not test whether demand levels predict the benefit of a scaffold per item at equal tokens, so gap 9 is only half answered. Demand labels come from an LLM annotator (GPT-4o).
agent_relevance: Demand profiles could route items to a scaffold or a plain call; nobody has measured the per-item scaffold gain, so that test has to be run by us.

source: Krakauer (2026) The Rise and Fall of G in AGI, epoch table (re-read in local text)
finding: Within-epoch PCA on four benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval) shows PC1 share and mean inter-test r peak in Epoch II and fall in the chain-of-thought epoch. But per-epoch n is tiny and the trend is not monotone.
numbers: Epoch I n=3: mean r .72, PC1 79%, eig2 1.24. Epoch II n=8: r .90, 92%, eig2 0.28. Epoch III n=7: r .73, 80%, eig2 0.49. Epoch IV n=4: r .43, 64%, eig2 1.88. Full matrix: 39 models x 14 benchmarks. Author says n=4 cannot be confirmed statistically.
limits: Epoch I (n=3) also has eig2 above 1, so the SLODR-like fall is not clean. With n of 3-8 and 4 variables, correlation matrices are nearly unestimable. Benchmarks saturate, which itself shrinks variance and correlations.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open from this source: the pattern is suggestive, not a test. A larger per-model matrix is needed (see d08-d10).

source: Krakauer (2026) partial correlations after removing PC1 (re-read in local text)
finding: After projecting out PC1 on five benchmarks (n=19), 7 of 10 residual correlations are negative (mean -0.24). The residuals split into a reasoning group (MATH, GPQA) and an execution/fluency group (GSM8K, HumanEval); MMLU stands alone.
numbers: 5 benchmarks, n=19 models with complete data. All 10 raw correlations positive. Mean residual r = -0.24.
quote: The positive manifold is entirely attributable to G.
limits: Residual correlations after removing a first component are negative by construction (they sum to near zero), so this is weak evidence of a real second factor. Same-lab models, benchmark saturation.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a depth-of-search versus recall split is seen here, but is partly arithmetic. Treat as a hypothesis for the router, not a finding.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) sample curation, Intelligence 106:101858 (local PDF text)
finding: The 591-model sample is only partly de-duplicated by family: DBSCAN on scores, then a manual look at names and parameter counts, then a name-similarity rule that drops pairs only if they also have the same parameter count. Fine-tunes of one base with different sizes or names survive.
numbers: 3862 -> 2680 (DBSCAN eps .33, min 2) -> 2415 (after removed models and a name clash) -> 1599 (manual, 816 dropped) -> 591 (Levenshtein threshold 20 plus same parameters). Authors report results were highly similar in the 2415, 1599 and 591 samples (supplement, not opened).
limits: No one-model-per-family sample exists in the paper. The check that g does not depend on family clustering is the 591 vs 2415 comparison, which is still family-contaminated.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: need an own test with one model per family (d08).

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) model fit: higher-order vs bifactor (local PDF text)
finding: Their planned second-order model (4 group factors under g) failed: negative residual variances. A one-factor ML model also fit poorly. The fitted bifactor model needed three correlated residuals to get close fit.
numbers: One factor TLI .814; two factors TLI .870, Hellaswag loading 1.07, factor r .78. Bifactor with 3 correlated residuals: chi2(44)=250.42, CFI .984, TLI .977, RMSEA .089 (above the .08 cutoff), SRMR .025. Mean g loading .81 (.64-.96), 65.6% variance, omega hierarchical .94; Gkn/Grw nested factor mean loading .50.
limits: Residuals were added after modification indices, so fit is partly tuned. RMSEA fails its own stated cutoff. Bifactor fit advantage is a known bias (Murray and Johnson, b10); the paper did not run a bias-corrected comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: partly answered. In LLM data the higher-order model did not even converge, and the bifactor was rescued by residual tuning. The Cucina and Byle advantage is not shown to hold or fail here.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) reliability and homogeneity caveat (local PDF text)
finding: Authors give two reasons the LLM g is stronger than human g: near-perfect score reliability and a narrow, similar set of tests. They did not measure run-to-run (test-retest) reliability.
numbers: Median internal consistency of the 12 composite scores 0.97, vs WAIS-IV subtest mean 0.88 (about .75-.80 in practice). No spatial test in the battery. They decline to call it artificial general intelligence.
limits: Internal consistency over hundreds of items is not test-retest. Sampling noise of 1000+ items is tiny, but run-to-run answer change is a separate source (see d13 and b25).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the noise ceiling on factor loadings from item sampling is high; the open part is run-to-run variance, which a scaffold may make worse or better.

source: Own computation (this session): Open LLM Leaderboard v2 contents, g share by sample design
finding: On 4,575 leaderboard models and 6 benchmarks (IFEval, BBH, MATH Lvl 5, GPQA, MUSR, MMLU-PRO), the first principal component is 73.5%. It stays 71-74% when models are cut down to one per base-model key, one per organisation, or the best per organisation.
numbers: All n=4575: PC1 73.5%, PC2 12.3%, mean r .67. Random one per Base Model key (n=3291, 300 draws): 73.1% (95% interval 73.0-73.2). Random one per organisation (n=715, 300 draws): 71.6% (70.4-72.6). Best model per organisation: 73.9%. Original non-merged weights n=3800: 74.0%. Official providers n=470: 71.1%. Loadings: IFEval .69, BBH .96, MATH .83, GPQA .89, MUSR .78, MMLU-PRO .96.
limits: Own PCA on normalised leaderboard scores (not factor analysis, so PC1 overstates common variance a little). Base Model column keys leave many fine-tune families un-merged; organisation dedup is coarse in the other direction. Six benchmarks, 5 mostly multiple choice, same leaderboard, snapshot dated 2025-03-20. Not peer reviewed; scripts in D:/research_scratch/A13.01/tmp/ (A13.01_run.py).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 mostly closed: family and duplicate covariance does not create the dominant first component. Family clustering lowers it by 1-2 points at most in this dataset.

source: Own computation (this session): leaderboard g share by ability band, size and date
finding: Splitting by ability does not reproduce a clean SLODR pattern. Both halves have lower PC1 than the whole sample, as range restriction predicts, and the top half is not lower than the bottom half.
numbers: Bottom half by Average: PC1 55.9%, mean r .44. Top half: 59.7%, r .42. Bottom quartile 41.0% (r .23); top quartile 54.7% (r .26). Parameters: 0-4B 65.1%, 4-9B 60.6%, 9-40B 70.3%, 40B+ 70.4%. Submitted 2024-06 onward: 73.4% (n=2661). One per Base Model halves: 57.0% bottom, 59.2% top.
limits: Splitting on the Average, which is built from the same 6 scores, truncates range and induces artefactual correlations (selection on a composite). Does not follow a same-model improvement path. The leaderboard ended in 2025, so frontier reasoning models are missing.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no sign of g falling with ability in this open-model sample. Krakauer's fall at the frontier (d03) is not contradicted, only not reproduced where the data are larger.

source: Own computation (this session): second component on the leaderboard
finding: PC2 is small overall (12.3%, eigenvalue .74) and contrasts instruction following (IFEval) with long-context reasoning (MUSR). In the top quartile, IFEval correlates negatively with MMLU-PRO.
numbers: All: PC2 loadings IFEval -.65, MUSR .46, GPQA .26, MATH -.20. Top quartile: IFEval vs MMLU-PRO r -.26 (full sample .65); PC2 loadings IFEval .67, MATH .61, MUSR -.33; eig2 1.08. Bottom quartile: IFEval vs MMLU-PRO r .19, eig2 1.41. BBH vs MMLU-PRO r .96 in the full sample.
limits: Top-quartile selection on the Average can create negative correlations (Berkson-type). Almost all tasks are multiple choice except IFEval and MATH, so a separate open-ended or reasoning factor cannot be separated from format here.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the only visible second axis is format or instruction following, not reasoning. This weakly supports Ilic's single g over a separable Gf for MC-style tests; it cannot refute Burnell.

source: Hendrycks et al. (2025) A Definition of AGI, protocol for long-term memory storage (local PDF text)
finding: The 0% scores for long-term memory storage are set by the test rules: items must be run in a new session after the information was shown, and external tools (search, retrieval) must be disabled. A stateless chat model scores zero by construction.
numbers: MS weight 10% (associative 4%, meaningful 3%, verbatim 3%). Both GPT-4 and GPT-5 score 0 in all three. Example items use 48 hours of intervening experiences. Total scores: GPT-4 27%, GPT-5 57%.
quote: External tools (e.g., internet search) must be disabled.
limits: The paper calls MS 'perhaps the most significant bottleneck' and also says RAG and long context are 'capability contortions'. The protocol excludes any scaffold with memory by design. The scoring is manual and no score is averaged over repeated runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: 0% is a protocol artefact in part: it measures the model not the system. A scaffold with a persistent store would score above zero under a system-level rule. This is the one profile gap a scaffold is built to close.

source: Hendrycks et al. (2025) scoring scope and tool rules across components (local PDF text)
finding: The definition is a set of manually graded tasks, not an automatic benchmark. Most components are tested text-in, text-out, tools off, no partial credit; at least one component allows search. No scaffold arm is reported.
numbers: Ten components, 10 points each. Testing notes found at several places: 'text input, text output; no partial credit. External tools are disabled', 'Text modality; search tools enabled', 'Tools disabled'. Table 1 GPT-4 8,6,4,0,2,0,4,0,0,3; GPT-5 9,10,10,7,4,0,4,4,6,3.
limits: Per-component profiles of two models only; no factor analysis and no scaffolded comparison. CHC mapping is by the authors, not validated by data.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: whether profile gaps predict scaffold gains is untested; the profile can only guide hypotheses, e.g. scaffold effort on R, WM, MR and V where scores are low and tool use is allowed.

source: Test-retest Reliability of Large Language Models and Their Concordance With Human Experts in Rubric-Based Scoring (2026, PMC13686340)
finding: At temperature 0, large closed models rescore the same item almost identically across 5 runs; a small open model is stable in total score but not in exact categories. Few-shot plus chain-of-thought prompting gave the best agreement with humans.
numbers: 122 statements x 6 rubric components, 4 LLMs x 5 runs x 4 prompts. Claude ICC and Fleiss kappa >= .99; GPT-4o and Mistral Large ICC >= .97, kappa >= .80 (except zero-shot); Mistral 7B ICC >= .88 but kappa .32-.52. Few-shot+CoT accuracy vs humans: Mistral Large 77%, Claude 71%, GPT-4o 67%, Mistral 7B 60%.
limits: A rating task on medical summaries, not an ability test, with temperature 0. It shows noise is low when sampling is greedy; b25 shows 42% of repeated items changed on a vocabulary test without that control (different setup). Not directly a ceiling on factor loadings.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: run-to-run noise is small at temperature 0 for strong models, so item sampling and model covariance matter more than retest noise. Scaffolds that sample (best-of-N) bring the noise back and should be tested for it.

source: Sources of Artifacts in SLODR Detection (Psychology in Russia, 2021, PMC10026998)
finding: Three moderated factor analysis methods could not separate a real SLODR dataset from simulated data with no SLODR but a different item-difficulty density or a skewed sample. Scale features can mask or fake the effect.
numbers: One real dataset plus three simulated sets matched on correlation matrix and skew (about -0.3). Review: Blum and Holling (2017) meta-analysis found the fall of correlations at higher g but only a little more than half of studies directly confirmed Spearman's hypothesis; Hartung et al. (2018) criticised that meta-analysis.
limits: Single dataset, simulation study. The meta-analytic numbers are as cited here, not re-opened in Blum and Holling.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: any SLODR test on benchmark percentages is open to scale artefacts (floors, ceilings). Use IRT-scaled abilities, as ADeLe does, before reading a fall in g as real.

source: McGrew (2023) Carroll's Three-Stratum Theory at 30 Years, J Intell 11(2):32 (PMC9959556)
finding: Carroll accepted a strong g and nine broad abilities in his last analyses; Horn held there is no g. Carroll rejected Horn's no-g model as a basis for denying g. McGrew recommends treating Cattell, Horn and Carroll as a family of CHC theories and comparing Carroll (g) with Horn (no g) structures.
numbers: Carroll 2003 analyses of 16- and 29-test WJ-R matrices: 1 g plus 9 broad factors, g loadings .28 to .78. McGrew's 2022 bifactor re-analysis of Carroll's 46-test solution: 1 g plus 10 broad, g loadings .25 to .86; 35 of 46 (76%) at or above .50 vs 18 of 29 (62%) in Carroll's. Strongest g loaders: acquired knowledge (Gc, Gq, Grw) and Gf.
quote: I cannot regard Horn's comment as a sound basis for denying the existence of a factor g
limits: Secondary reading of Carroll by the main CHC author; the 461 data-set count of the 1993 survey is not stated in this paper. Horn's view is relayed, not Horn's own text.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: partly closed. Primary-level numbers on Carroll's structure now in hand (9-10 broad, one g, knowledge tests load highest); 461 stays secondary. For the agent: broad-ability labels are working categories, not settled causes.

source: McGrew (2023) Carroll's own doubts about g
finding: Carroll after 1993 said it was unproven that g is more than a statistical product. Quoted by McGrew from Carroll 1997 and 1998.
numbers: Quotes: 1998 p.13 asks whether 'a factorially produced g is merely a mathematical artifact'; 1997 says that g as a true ability independent of specific abilities 'has not been adequately demonstrated and proven'.
quote: the question remains whether a unitary g exists, or whether a factorially produced g is merely a mathematical artifact
limits: Quoted second hand through McGrew; context of the original passages not read.
agent_relevance: Supports using g as a descriptive index of the benchmark manifold, not as a causal trait, when applied to LLMs.

source: Wilson et al. (2023) CHC cross-national paper, description of Carroll (re-read)
finding: Introductions in the CHC literature describe Carroll's survey as a factor analysis of 'over 450 data sets'. This is a count restated, not checked against Carroll's book.
numbers: 'over 450 data sets' (Carroll 1993). Other sources in this folder say 461.
quote: the factor analysis of over 450 data sets that led to a hierarchical model
limits: Secondary; rounding differs between sources. Carroll 1993 full text is lending-only on archive.org (HTTP 401) and was not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: keep '461' flagged as secondary and use 'over 450' in agent-facing text.

source: Existing evidence recheck: Ruan et al. (2024) sample design (c09 text) and Maimon (a19) sample
finding: Both of the other large LLM factor studies already include several models per family, so neither answers the family-covariance question. Ruan: 77 models from 21 families (about 3.7 per family) with PC1 about 80%; Maimon: 60 models, 8 factors.
numbers: Ruan 77 models, 21 families, PC1 about 80%, top 3 PCs about 97%. Maimon 60 x 44 matrix, 8 factors, 85% cumulative variance rule.
limits: Taken from evidence lines c09 and a19 (opened earlier), not re-read this pass.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the 72-74% from d08 fits inside the 65.6-85% spread; family clustering is not the cause of the spread. Task mix and model range are.
